speechtext:
In making an announcement respecting pension legislation I may say that several features have been taken into consideration. In the first place the Pension Act that was originally drawn up in 1919 was amended in 1920, 1921, 1922, 1923, 1924, and 1925. On several occasions these amendments were the result of long deliberation by special parliamentary committees appointed for the purpose, and on one occasion the result of a protracted investigation of general reestablishment measures by a royal commission appointed in 1922, the final report of that commission being submitted to the government as late as 1924. The important feature of all the above is that the Pension Act has received the very close attention of parliament during past years.
This year there have been presented to me by various soldier organizations, resolutions asking mainly for additional benefits to be provided by change in the regulations of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment and the Board of Pension Commissioners, and additional benefits to be provided under the Pension Act. The total number of these resolutions is approaching two hundred, of which more than fifty suggest changes in the pension legislation.
I also call the attention of the House to the fact that there was recently inserted in the Pension Act a meritorious clause under which cases of real merit or hardship can be awarded pension at the discretion of the Board of Pension Commissioners and the Federal Appeal Board, even though such cases are not provided for under the ordinary terms of the Pension Act. I may say that already a number of pensions have been awarded under this provision.
I do not think the members and the country generally fully appreciate the nature and extent of the numerous proposals which have been made. Many of these suggestions involve ramifications which can be foreseen only after careful and detailed examination. There are extended commitments involved and there must be a thorough canvass of the effect on other classes not dealt with. It would be apparent I think to anyone who read the accumulation of material which has come to me during this session that there could be no fair opportunity during a session of parliament for the government to give the con-

Privilege-Mr. Beaubien
sideration and thought which matters of this kind deserve. I may say that in the recess, attention will be given to the practicability of a consolidation of the Pension Act, and these proposals involving statutory changes will be considered in that connection.
In the meantime, I think that some of the suggestions may be found to be quite possible of being dealt with by administrative rather than legislative action and I propose to consider that method of procedure.
I can also say, and I feel sure that this will be regarded as of very great importance by those who are interested in these matters, that while the government cannot at this session consider extending the principles upon which pensions are granted, they have under consideration amendments relating more or less to procedure, one of which will deal with the extension for a further term of two years of the period within which applications for pensions may be received. It is my purpose to move this amendment when bill No. 234 is again in committee.

Mr. Chairman, I wish simply to state my objection also to this bill. It purports to take from the courts the power of declaring when a company is insolvent. Under the Winding-up Act the insolvency of a company is always a matter for judicial decision, and, before that decision is given, all parties in interest are afforded an opportunity to be heard in a judicial proceeding, whereupon judgment is given as to whether it has been clearly shown that the company is insolvent and should be wound up. This bill, together with the Insurance Act of 1917, makes it impossible for a company to carry on business except under an annual license from the department. I think that is a wrong departure, and that it is very likely ultra vires of this parliament to enact such provisions. As to whether the act of 1917 in that respect is within the powers of the parliament of Canada to enact should be judicially determined at the earliest possible date. At the present time there is a majority decision of the highest appellate court of Ontario declaring that similar licensing provisions are ultra vires. But the second point is this. When an official of the Department of Finance has declared that in his opinion the license of the company should not be renewed, the fact of the official's refusal to renew the license is taken as evidence, complete and final, that the company is insolvent. In such a case it no longer remains a matter for judicial decision as to whether the company is or is not insolvent; it is in fact decided to be insolvent by an official of the department who is utterly unqualified to exercise such a discretion, and who has not the judicial experience necessary to enable him to decide the question. I admit at once that this matter has passed the standing committee, but I regard it as most pernicious legislation in this respect. I think it is far better that the decision as to whether a company is solvent or insolvent should be

left entirely to the courts; it should not depend upon a discretionary decision, as to the renewal of the license, to be given by an official of the department who, as I say, is without experience, or to be given by any political agency such as the government of the country or any department thereof.

Section agreed to.

speechtext:
Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to amend the act respecting the Department of Marine and Fisheries to provide that the department shall consist of the

Post Office Act
Marine branch and the Fisheries branch, and that two officers may be appointed by the governor in council as Deputy Minister of Marine and Deputy Minister of '.Fisheries, respectively.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Johnston in the chair.

subtopic: DIVISION INTO TWO BRANCHES WITH SEPARATE DEPUTY MINISTERS
speechtext: Is it the intention to appoint to the position of Deputy Minister of Fisheries an official presently in the employ of the department or some outside person?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DIVISION INTO TWO BRANCHES WITH SEPARATE DEPUTY MINISTERS
speechtext: Beyond saying that the government will endeavour to make' the best appointment possible, I am afraid I cannot give my hon. friend any information.

subtopic: DIVISION INTO TWO BRANCHES WITH SEPARATE DEPUTY MINISTERS
speechtext: That of course is no answer at all. I should like to know. A great deal of the good that we hope will come from this division of the department and the setting up of a new Deputy Minister of Fisheries will depend upon the person of the official appointed. If it is intended to make a political appointment, we shall not gain the effect that was intended to be gained by the Duncan report. If behind this move there is the intention to do what the members of the Duncan commission sought to accomplish, a great deal of good will be achieved and I heartily endorse the proposal. I believe that to be the crux of the situation. If a political appointment is to be made, the purpose of the legislation will be defeated. If the reverse is the case, I will welcome the legislation and I am sure it will be welcomed by the maritimes.

We have too many political heads of departments in Canada now and the cabinet could very well be reduced in numbers. I think the Prime Minister, in some lucid moments which he has had in days gone by, has agreed to that proposal He would like to reduce the number, but political exigency and expediency are such that, instead of the number of portfolios in this country being Teduced, they are constantly being increased, with the result that we are top-heavy in the departments of government. subtopic: POSTAGE BATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS

speechtext:
Hon. P. J. VENIOT (Postmaster General) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to amend the Post Office Act and to reduce the postage rate on certain newspapers and periodicals from one and one-half cents to one cent.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Johnston in the chair.

subtopic: POSTAGE BATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext: Is the rate per one hundred pounds or per pound?

subtopic: POSTAGE BATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext: Per pound.

subtopic: POSTAGE BATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Will the Postmaster
General kindly explain the purport of the resolutions and also what classes of newspapers and periodicals it applies to?

subtopic: POSTAGE BATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Under the present act certain classes of newspapers and periodicals are
Post Office Act

charged one and one-half cents a pound. Subsection (3) of section 53 of the old act reads:
Newspapers and periodicals which are required to be transmitted for a greater distance than is mentioned in the last preceding section

That is forty miles.
[DOT]-or the publication of which is of greater frequency than once a week, and the newspapers and periodicals described in the immediately preceding sub-section, upon any copies in excess of the circulation of 2,500 copies, shall be subject to postage at the rate of three-quarters of a cent on and after the first day of January, one thousand nine hundred and twenty-one, and until the first day of January, one thousand nine hundred and twenty-two, and one and one-half cents thereafter, for each pound weight or any fraction of a pound weight, and such postage shall be prepaid by postage stamps or otherwise as the Postmaster General from time to time directs.
With reference to those newspapers and periodicals, the rate is changed from one and one-half cents to one cent per pound.

subtopic: POSTAGE BATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext: Will that reduce the rate below the cost of carriage?

subtopic: POSTAGE BATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext: The rate is somewhat below the cost of carriage now. I may say that the reason for this is that the Post Office Department is losing revenue because owing to the high rate of one and one-half cents per pound for delivery of newspapers specified in subsection 3, the large dailies especially are now using motor trucks to deliver their papers for a distance of thirty and forty miles, and in some cases they are sending large parcels by freight, and in other cases by express. W ith the rate reduced to one cent a pound, the post office will get an increased volume of business because these papers will refrain from using these motor trucks in order to send these parcels out. We anticipiate that the revenue will be increased, owing to the volume carried, to such an extent that whatever deficit there may be at the present time will not be increased.

subtopic: POSTAGE BATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Do you not carry them
free now up to forty miles?

subtopic: POSTAGE BATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Not these papers; weeklies.
I will read the section that refers to the other class of newspapers:
(2) Newspapers and periodicals published not more frequently than once a week in any city, town or village which has a population of not more than ten thousand persons shall be entitled to be transmitted by mail free of postage to the extent of a circulation of 2,500 copies per issue within a distance of forty miles from their place of publication.

Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Veniot thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 259, to amend the Post Office Act.

Motion agreed to, bill read the first and second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 1-Postage rates on certain newspapers and periodicals reduced from 1\ cents to one cent.

subtopic: POSTAGE BATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, will you kindly see that the bill is distributed before we proceed?

subtopic: POSTAGE BATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext: The bills have been printed; they should be distributed, but as apparently they are not, I am willing to move that the committee rise.

subtopic: POSTAGE BATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext: I am not objecting to this proposed change in the law at all, but I want to comment on what the hon. minister said when we were in committee on the resolution. We are carrying these papers now for one cent and a half a pound at a loss, and the minister puts up the argument that by carrying them for one cent we are not going to make so big a loss. It may be true that with this decreased rate the newspapers will not use motor trucks so much or send so many of their newspapers by express, but it is an extraordinary argument to say that because you are losing money carrying them for one cent and a half, you will carry them for one cent, in order not to lose so much. The hon. gentleman would never apply that principle to any private business that he controlled himself. He would never say in regard to his own business: In order to reduce my loss, I am going to carry these papers for one cent; in that way I shall do a larger volume of business, and my loss will be less than it is now.

subtopic: POSTAGE BATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext: I can give the hon. gentleman an example in connection with the Post Office Department. Before the letter postage was reduced some years ago from three cents to two cents, there was a defiicit in the Post Office Department, but inside of two years from decreasing the rate there was a surplus of $450,000, owing to the increased volume of business, and that is what I anticipate in this connection.

subtopic: POSTAGE BATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext:
I submit that
that is hardly a fair argument, because you were not paying the railways all the revenue you were getting for carrying the letters. The

Dominion Elections Act
reason that you had a deficit there was that you had not enough business. You were not paying the railways more than you were getting from the public for carrying their letters, but in this case you are paying the railways more than you are getting from the newspapers for carrying their papers.

subtopic: POSTAGE BATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext: We are not paying the railways more exactly. If the hon. gentleman understood the situation better, he would not object. The whole of the cost is not the railway transportation. It is in the distribution by rail and otherwise through the Post Office Department. The railway transportation is not the whole cost.

subtopic: POSTAGE BATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext:
If I understand the
working of the minister's department correctly, the low rate given for the distribution of magazines, catalogues, and such like is applicable for a distance of thirty or forty miles, and in my town I have seen carloads of magazines coming by train and motor truck and being dumped into the post office, making a large amount of extra work for which the officials of the post office are not being paid anything extra, and through which the country must lose a considerable revenue. I would ask the minister if he has ever considered modifying that regulation in order to increase the revenue of his department.

subtopic: POSTAGE BATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext: AVhile I was considering this amendment I had a discussion with some of our mail superintendents along those very lines, and the matter is being looked into, but I am not in a position to state that anything definite will be done this session. I think there are certain privileges granted under the Post Office Act that ought to be modified in regard to the distribution not only of certain periodicals but of advertising matter as well

subtopic: POSTAGE BATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext:
I would suggest to the
Postmaster General that, when the bill comes before the committee again, he have such information at his hand as can be obtained in the department, to show what the carrying of newspapers costs this country as well as any loss sustained.

subtopic: POSTAGE BATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext: I can give that information now, but perhaps I had better wait until the matter is before the House again.

subtopic: POSTAGE BATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext: Would the minister obtain the cost of carrying on the business of the mail order houses, which are greatly injuring the retail trade of this country?

subtopic: POSTAGE BATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext: There is no greater privilege given to the mail order houses than is given to any other wholesale or retail stores for their mail order business.

subtopic: POSTAGE BATES ON NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Except it is given for
limited distribution.
Progress reported.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND SALARY OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER

speechtext:
Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Dominion Elections Act and to provide that the chief electoral officer shall be appointed by resolution of the House of Commons, and shall be paid a salary of six thousand dollars per annum.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Johnston in the chair.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND SALARY OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
I would like a word of
explanation.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND SALARY OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
The Dominon Elections
Act, section 19, says:
Air. Oliver Mowat Biggar, of the city of Ottawa, one of His Majesty's counsel, is hereby appointed Chief Electoral Officer.
Colonel Biggar, as every hon. member of the House will agree, has given full satisfaction in the performance of his duties. He has intimated to the government that he intends to relinquish his post, and notwithstanding representations made to him, he has persisted in that intention. Therefore it is now necessary to provide for his successor. The section of the act naming him as Chief Electoral Officer will require to be amended, in order that we may now appoint someone to perform his duties. The bill which will be introduced following this resolution will have two objects; first, to see that in future the Chief Electorial Officer shall be appointed, not by the government but by the House of Commons, and a resolution will be introduced this session to provide for the appointment of a person to replace Colonel Biggar. The present Chief Electoral Officer is in receipt of a salary of $12,000 a year, the salary now paid to a judge of the Supreme court, having the same standing as a judge of the Supreme court, by the wording of the act. Besides his duties as Chief Electoral Officer, paragraph (d) of section 19 says:
Dominion Elections Act

Subject to the performance of the foregoing duties, act as counsel for the crown or the attorney general in such causes, prepare such opinions, and make such inquiries as the Governor in Council may from time to time direct.
It is not the intention of the government to require the new Chief Electoral Officer, in addition to his duties as Chief Electoral Officer, to perform duties as counsel for the government, and that is the reason why the salary, instead of being $12,000, will be reduced to $6,000.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND SALARY OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext: When the present Elections Act was passed in the House, I think in 1921, I happened to have charge of it, and I remember well this section under which the Chief Electoral Officer was originally appointed. He was appointed, I might inform the committee, under practically a joint arrangement or recommendation made between myself, representing the then government, and my right hon. friend representing the then opposition. I remember that we consulted in regard to the person who should be appointed to this position, and it was mutually agreed that Colonel Biggar would be an admirable man. I suggest to the government that there should be some consultation before any names are submitted in the present instance, and I fancy the government will probably follow that course, because I realized when the original act was passed that we were laying down a principle for the future. It is very important that the person appointed to fill this position should not only be an outstanding man, as far as possible removed from party politics, but a man who has the confidence of all panties in the House. I am satisfied there are many such available for the position. In the case of Colonel Biggar it was considered at that time that, as the government had a great deal of litigation, it would be an excellent thing to have a man who could be utilized as government counsel. I do not know that the work in that respect is as great now as it was after the conclusion of the war, and the necessity for having a government counsel may not exist at the present time to such an extent at all events as it did at that time. I would also suggest to the government, that when they come to the question of selecting the appointee, the principle of promotion should not be overlooked. With these remarks I have no objection to the resolution being carried in its present form.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND SALARY OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
I might say
that I agree entirely with the hon. the leader of the opposition as Ito the coarse of

procedure. The intention of the government is to have a conference in advance between the leaders of the parties, and if possible to agree upon a name. I also agree with my hon. friend that where it is possible to recognize merit in the appointment this should be done.
With respect to the services of government counsel I might say that the government would hesitate to dispense with the professional services of Colonel Biggar, were it not that the Solicitor General has undertaken to carry on the work performed by Colonel Biggar as government counsel. I think it advisable to let the House know that the hon. the Solicitor General is undertaking, on behalf of the government much of the professional work which formerly was assigned to the Chief Electoral Officer.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND SALARY OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
What will be the tenure
of office of the new appointee? Is that regulated by the existing statute, or will it be regulated by the amendment?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND SALARY OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
It will be the same as heretofore.
Mr^GUTHRIE: His tenure of office is the same as that of a Supreme court judge; he is removable only on an address to parliament.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND SALARY OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext: Does the government intend to amend any other part of the Elections Act?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND SALARY OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext: Not this session.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND SALARY OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext: I have the bill here. The only change, in section 19, as pointed out by the leader of the opposition, will be in relation to Colonel Biggar, stating that the Chief Electoral Officer will be appointed by a resolution of the House of Commons. Therefore the Chief Electoral Officer will remain in office according to the remaining paragraph of the section.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND SALARY OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
Having regard to the fact that the Chief Electoral Officer has the status of a Supreme court judge, does the Prime Minister think that he can get a man for the salary of $6,000 who would be of such character and standing as to command the confidence of the whole country?
Mr. MiACKENZIE KING: The status of a Supreme court judge had reference, I think, to the circumstance that Colonel Biggar was recognized as having a very high standing in his profession. The present intention is to

Civil Service Superannuation Act
have regard primarily to the capability of the appointee to fill the position of Chief Electoral Officer, not the position as well of government counsel.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT

speechtext:
Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture) moved the second reading of Bill No. 229 to amend the Live Stock and Live Stock Products Act, 1923.

Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 231, to amend the Civil Service Superannuation Act, 1924.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 1-"Misconduct."

Mr. Chairman, for the
benefit of those who were not here when the resolution preceding this bill was introduced, will the minister be good enough to state shortly its purport?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes. The bill is to correct
some of the anomalies and defects that have developed since the act was passed three years ago. The time for taking advantage of the act is extended' to July of this year. My hon. friend will recall that a measure for this purpose was brought in last session, but failed to pass the Senate.

Is there any extension of
the principle of superannuation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

Mr. Chairman, is it
proposd to extend superannuation to officers in the government marine service? I understand that those officers are not included in the civil service, nor have they the benefit of superannuation or pensions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps progress will be expedited by my explaining to the House that the superannuation scheme is based on contributions by civil servants, which are calculated on an actuarial basis. Any departure from the scheme will add to the cost; for instance, if the scope of the act should be widened in such a way as to change the prospective length of service basis. Such a departure would be brought about by including employees occupying obviously temporary positions liable to be terminated at any time; employees paid otherwise than on the basis of a stated annual salary; employees occupying positions which, though technically permanent, are not so. In other words, the act is not intended to include any employees whose sudden withdrawal from the service would impose unexpected demands on the funds. If the basis of the superannuation scheme were widened as I have stated, or in any other way not contemplated by the framers of the act, then undoubtedly it would be necessary either to increase the amount of contributions by the civil servants or for the government to bear a larger proportion than one-half the total cost of the scheme. So my hon. friend will see that to do what he suggests would be unfair to those who are already contributing to the scheme.

Do lighthouse keepers
come under this act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, those who are permanent.
On what basis are they retired?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I know that a number of lighthouse keepers have to engage help and they have asked for an allowance on the basis of the contribution they have made, taking into account what they have paid out to their assistants during the season. The Department of Justice rules that this would not be actuarially sound and would not be fair to minor employees.

In such case how would the minister compute a fair salary to the lighthouse keeper himself in view of the fact that he has had to pay for help? Do you get a return from him showing what he has paid out?

Civil Service Superannuation Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The computation is made on the basis of a return from the Department of Marine and Fisheries regarding the salary actually due the head lighthouse keeper himself.

I understand that in the case of civil servants on the permanent staff who went overseas their absence during military service is counted in computing their superannuation. I believe that is correct. This however is not true of those on the temporary list, even though such employees may have been in the service of the government ten years or longer; the time they served overseas is not counted towards their superannuation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is my hon. friend referring to employees on the permanent staff?

I first stated what I understood to be the condition regarding permanent employees and I am contrasting that with the position of the non-permanent men. Although a man may have been in the service of the government for many years-ten years or more-the time he put in during the war is not counted, notwithstanding that he was given leave of absence by the department. It seems to me there is a good deal to be said for these temporary employees.
Does this bill make provision for men in the outside service, such as lock and bridge tenders, at the Welland canal?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If they are on the permanent staff and come within the range of salary, and if they comply with other conditions relating to contributions.
What about those holding seasonal positions?
Has the minister no comment to make on the point to which I have called his attention?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
All these cases are considered by the Department of Justice, who advise the department administering the act. On December 16, 1920, there was passed an order in council which was amended on October 31, 1921, laying down general regulations to give permanency, by means of what was known as the blanketing process, to temporary employees. That order in council remained in force until 1924 when the Civil Service Commission advised that it had been in operation long enough and should be rescinded. It was therefore cancelled. I know there has been some criticism of this blanketing method;

those who were not included in the process at that time now claim to have a grievance. Let me direct the attention of the committee to certain provisions of the bill. Subsections 5 and 6 of section 8 provide:
(v)	periods of past non-contributory service in or under any branch or portion of the public service of Canada which had ceased to exist prior to the coming into force of this act shall be counted for the purposes of this act.
(vi)	persons whose duties or employment are of a seasonal character shall be deemed to be civil servants within the meaning of this act and eligible to be contributors thereunder and their periods of work and of lay-off from the works shall be counted for the purpose of computing any allowance or gratuity under this act.
The foregoing provisions will, I think, meet the views advanced by my hon. friends.

I would submit the case of another class of employees, the caretakers of armouries under the Department of National Defence. Many of these men have been in the service of the government for twenty years and are to all intents and purposes permanent employees; yet they are compelled to submit to the injustice of having to .put in a renewed application every six months for the positions they hold. I know of one man in Kingston who has been for twenty years in the one position and whom nobody would think for a moment of replacing. Surely such an employee ought to be made permanent.

Perhaps the Minister of
National Defence (Mr. Ralston) will give some information regarding these caretakers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I should like to be advised
in the matter. Do they work all day or only part of the time? We have not heard about it before.
They are permanently employed day in and day out, living in the armouries.
A long list of such cases has been submitted to me and I am trying if possible to find some means of putting this class of employees on a more permanent basis.

After the announcement
made by the Secretary of State to-day I consider this a red letter day for government employees.
First of April.

Civil servants are to
receive increases ranging from $60 to $120 and I wish now to speak for a class of employees

Civil Service Superannuation Act
of whom there are a good many in my constituency. These people have served the government faithfully for a good many years, some of them for a quarter of a century. They did not contribute to any pensions fund and now they are left without any resource, and the government seems unable to do anything for these faithful servants. I should like to ask the minister whether it would not be possible to do something at the present time for people who had been in the employ of the government for fifteen, twenty or twenty-five years, but who did not contribute a penny to any superannuation fund, and are now practically penniless? Is there no authority under which provision can be made for such cases?
There is the Old Age Pension Act.

But I am referring to
persons who are government employees. There are many such cases all over Canada, and I want to know from the Minister of Finance if there is not some authority in the existing laws whereby provision can be made for some of these cases?
What particular class?

I have in mind the case
of one man who was agent on an Indian reserve for twenty or twenty-five years. He was a permanent official, but he was not asked to contribute anything to any superannuation fund. Now he is in straitened circumstances, and I thought there might be a provision in the law somewhere to take care of such a case as that. I understand that in the case of former ministers of the crown the Treasury Board has power to investigate when they are in necessitous circumstances and come to their relief. I was wondering whether it would not be possible, either under the existing law or by means of an amendment, to provide for cases of the particular nature that I have indicated.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not know of any such
provision in the act nor would I care to recommend the enactment of such a provision. I think it would be a very dangerous power to confer. The Treasury Board might be met with importunities that would be hard to resist politically and that could not be met on any sound actuarial basis.
With respect to the observations of my hon. friend from Kingston (Mr. Ross) that matter is under review. We shall have to see whether we can devise some method of treating such cases fa.irly, but I cannot make any commitment at the present time.
It is a very worthy case.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes.
Mr. MoGIBBON:	I would draw the attention of the minister to the situation of a class of postmasters in this country who have been working on commission. I have in mind one such postmaster who has been in the service of the country for nearly sixty years. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I quite appreciate the position of my hon. friend's postmaster because I recall that at one time, when the present Speaker was Postmaster General, I brought to his attention the case of a postmaster in my own riding who claimed that he was the oldest living postmaster in Canada. However, under the act he could do nothing for that man at that time, and we cannot do anything now because these men do not come within the class of cases in which superannuation is allowed.

I was chairman of the
committee that made the recommendation on which the act was based. The act was designed to meet the case of new entrants to the service, but provision was made to allow those contributing under the previous superannuation acts to come in upon paying the difference in the contributions. At the time referred to strong representations were made with respect to unusual oases such as those to which the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Ross) and the hon. member for Muskoka (M|r. McGibbon) have called attention, but those to whom the framing of the act was entrusted felt that the measure would be jeopardized if an attempt was made to provide for all such cases. I recall representations on behalf of some such servant as the hon. member for Kingston has spoken of, but he was under the Militia department and that department had its own pension system. I think there is a good deal to be said on behalf of old caretakers, however, and if the Superintendent of Insurance could frame a suitable amendment I would be glad to see the minister adopt it because the committee were certainly sympathetic to such cases.

I ask the minister
whether he does not think that it is in the interests of the public that cases of the kind I have indicated should be looked after. Men of that age cannot live very much longer; it is inevitable that they should disappear before very long. It does seem to me that something ought to be done to provide for persons in such a situation.

Supplementing what I have already said the Indian agent in the case to which I have referred was appointed at $150 a year. The present occupant of the office will probably benefit by a pension, whereas his predecessor who worked for half the present salary may have to be looked after by the municipality. Certainly something should be done for this man who has reached the advanced age of over eighty. It is a poor object lesson to the people of Canada if, when the time comes for them to retire, we cannot provide for those who served the country so long and so faithfully and upon the low salaries that then prevailed.

The minister
spoke of those under the old superannuation acts having to pay the difference between the contribution fixed by the old acts and that fixed by the present law. I believe civil servants have to pay not only that difference, but also four per cent on the arrears. This has kept many civil servants from coming under the new superannuation law. Although they would be able to pay the amount of the difference they feel that they cannot pay interest on the arrears and live decently. Is there no way by which the government can do away with the provision requiring the payment of four per cent interest so that all the members of the civil service can come under the Superannuation Act? I think the government will find that in time it would pay them if they did that. Then all the civil servants would be under the new act. At present the)' are not, and some day the government will have to provide in some other way for those who have not come under the act.

In reply to my hon.
friend may I say that the act as worked out by the committee was placed on an actuarial basis, one-half being contributed by the employee and one-half by the state. That made it very difficult to consider the case of a man who had never paid anything into the fund. Such a man could never be expected to pay five per cent of his total salary for

the whole period in which he was in the government service because he would not likely be in a position to make such a heavy payment. At the time the act passed this House, with very strong support on both sides, it was felt that as it had been worked out on an actuarial basis there was no further need for contributions by civil servants other than those for which the measure provides. The upper chamber however felt that there was, and that those who were under the old scheme and coming into the new, were not contributing sufficient to the new scheme. The upper chamber therefore amended the bill by making necessary the payment of 4 per cent simple interest. They did not ask that it be compounded. I do not know what influence my hon. friend has in the upper chamber. He has some relatives there, and I would suggest that he get his relatives to introduce a bill in the upper chamber and to endeavour to have the upper chamber accept the bill as it was passed by this House.

I should like to
make some remarks on clause 4 if we are to take them clause by clause. As regards clause 1, many civil servants suffer because a charge is made against them, perhaps by some head of a department, and they do not have a trial. I am a great believer in the fairness of something like a court martial, so that when a man is charged with misconduct he has an appeal or a hearing before he suffers directly from the charge.

I would like to draw
the attention of the minister to what I consider an injustice in the administration of the present Superannuation Act. A man entering the employ of the government and being dismissed or leaving it in less than ten years is not eligible to secure a refund of the money which he has paid into this fund. I have had referred to me a particular case which the minister now has in his hands, showing how this injustice works out. This man was employed as a farm instructor for a period of nearly five years, and the very fact that he was in the government employ for that length of time would indicate that his services were reasonably satisfactory. He was however dismissed. I am not familiar with the reason why he was dismissed, but he is to-day in a very unfortunate position. His wife is sick in the hospital; he is without work and without a dollar, and yet the very considerable amount of money which he has paid into this fund cannot be returned to him. I admit that this is not covered by the act, but it is covered by a ruling made by the

Civil Service Superannuation Act
Treasury Board in conformity with the act. I would like to ask the minister if there is any possibility of a change being made in this ruling of the Treasury Board so that cases of this kind may be dealt with and justice rendered to the parties concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hpn. friend will recall that under the old act a man retiring at any time, and under the present act a man retiring in less than ten years, cannot get a refund. My hon. friend will observe that even in the good civil sendee of Canada we have discovered some employees who could not get a refund if they retired voluntarily, but who, knowing that they might if they were dismissed, invited dismissal for the purpose of securing a refund. This provision is for the purpose of clearing that up.

That hardly deals with
the case to which I am referring. It makes no material difference whether this was in the old act or in the new. The point is that an absolute injustice was done to this man. He perhaps may not want to pay into the fund but he is compelled to do so. He has no alternative, and yet when he is dismissed from the service, or leaves the service through apparently no fault of his, so far as I can understand, or at least does not leave the service voluntarily, a considerable portion of his salary is confiscated. Actually 5 per cent of that man's salary over a period of four and a half years service has been confiscated. That is practically a dishonest proceeding.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Is my hon. friend arguing
on behalf of the taxpayers of his constituency or on behalf of some particular employee?

I am arguing in reference to this particular case, but in a general way I am asking for justice for any employee who may be placed in a similar position. If contributions to the civil service fund were voluntary: if this man went into it understanding that he was paying the money voluntarily, taking his chances of losing it later, I could quite understand in that case he would have to be prepared to lose if he were dismissed or left the service within ten years. I would like to ask the Minister of Railways what an employee of the Canadian National Railways would say if 5 per cent or any particular amount were deducted from his salary and kept in a fund of this kind, and nothing returned to him under such circumstances.
That is the exact principle underlying the provident fund in connection with the Intercolonial.

Is no refund made to
those men?
Mr. DLTNN1NG: The only fund we have is the Intercolonial provident fund and it is conducted on this very principle.

The employees of the
whole railway would not stand for anything of that kind.
They do.

It is most unjust. If contributions to the fund were voluntary, I would see no injustice; but when they are compulsory, you might just as well pay the man that much less salary in the first place because when he has left the service through no particular fault of his own, he cannot get a refund.

My hon. friend, in
making such a statement as he does, is certainly very poorly informed in regard to the principle of superannuation acts. There is a great difference between an annuity whereby a man gets back the money paid in, plus some small rate of interest, and an insurance policy under which he may win a large amount of money or to which he may be a heavy contributor and lose. If some did not lose there could not be the returns paid that are paid to civil servants who put in the full thirty-five years service, receive the superannuation of 70 per cent, and live for many years afterwards. Every superannuation scheme in existence;, the New York Central scheme, the New Zealand act, the Canadian Pacific superannuation act, were considered by the committee, and this act as recommended was a combination of the opinions of the men on that committee as covering most fully the views representative of all parties in the House and also of the men administering superannuation acts which were outstandingly good in America.'
Were the employees consulted and were they satisfied?

Representatives of men's organizations by the score were in front of us. We had actuarial advice on this plan. If a man does not want to come into the civil service on a contributory plan, he does not have to do so. Under the old act a man contributed to a plan and he got certain refunds, but the state was contributing nothing. The hon. member for Mackenzie cannot show me an act based on the principle of superannuation whereby a man is allowed to elect to make it an annuity. If a man goes into the scheme, puts in his

full period of service, retires and lives for many years, he is bound to get out more than he puts in. If a man after putting in his full period of service retires, draws the superannuation and lives only one year, of course an injustice is done; he never gets back all the money he has paid in. The same thing is true of life insurance. All life insurance is bound to benefit some more than others. The principle of the thing is to benefit the civil servant who lives a long time so that in his old age he will not be in want. The act also takes care of widows to the extent of 50 per cent of the superannuation of the civil servant and there is a grant of so much for each child. None of these benefits could possibly come to retiring civil servants if there were not some sources of revenue beyond the actual contributions. All cannot possibly take out with interest what they pay in under this scheme.
If the contributions to the widows and orphans are largely made up by taking the money from men like this, an injustice is certainly done.
No.

I asked if the employees
were satisfied to come under the act.

It was the civil servants of Canada who requested this act, and they were all delighted when it was brought into force. We were pressed week after week and month after month by the civil servants themselves to bring down this act. They wanted it, and they are stall pressing for further amendments.

That might all be true; nobody is denying it, but the principle raised by the hon. member for Mackenzie is the injustice done to a man who has been in the service five or more years and may be forced out. That is a different matter altogether. I can tell the hon. minister that there was a time when life insurance companies took that stand, but they do not do it to-day; they dare not do it.
Which stand?

The stand of retaining
the premiums of those who dropped their insurance. No insurance company would dare do that to-day. I think the point raised by the hon. member for Mackenzie is absolutely sound. You should not rob one man to pay another. It is not just that a man who has been paying into the fund for a number of years should lose everything he has put in if, for some reason or other, he is forced out

or has to drop out of the service. Nothing under heaven can justify that. If the state is not contributing enough to enable those who remain in the service to get a pension, it is its duty to contribute more. It is not fair to make a levy on the man who for one cause or another is forced to drop out of the service after contributing to the fund for a number of years. As I said before, life insurance companies once took that stand and retained the premiums of those who dropped out, but they do not do it to-day.

The life insurance
company makes no contribution; it all comes from the individual. But in this case the government contributes as well as the civil servants, and all the contributions go into a general fund to pay the pensions of those who remain in the service.
You never help the man whose money you retain.

No, we help the other
man who stays on.

You are retaining his
contributions unjustly.

We do not retain his
contributions. They all go into the fund for the benefit of other civil servants who stay in the service.

The man is the loser.
There is no justice in that.

There is no justice in
superannuation anyway.
If a bank dismisses one of its servants, they pay him what he has contributed into the pension fund, plus interest, and I submit that that case is on all fours with this.

No, it is different. My hon. friend surely knows that in connection with the Superannuation Act which was brought down, and which civil servants were so desirous of having brought into force, they are quite prepared that some shall be losers for the benefit of those that stay on. When the civil servants make their contributions for the first ten years, the state makes an equal contribution. < The $10,000,000 or $12,000,000 that was in the old civil service fund was transferred to this new fund, and many of the men who were under the old scheme dropped out without any benefit whatever. There cannot be one hundred per cent justice in superannuation, because some will win more than others, and if one man wins, some other man must lose. If you want to

Civil Service Superannuation Act
have a return of contributions to those who drop out of the service, which was never discussed before the committee by the civil servants who were pressing for this bill, there would have to be a heavier levy both upon the employee and upon the government. This Superannuation Act was worked out practically on the principle of the New Zealand superannuation act, modified by some clauses in the Canadian Pacific Railway and New York Central acts, and in every instance the civil servants themselves were pressing for the bill to be brought into force.
The minister contradicted me, but he has not said one word to justify his contradiction. I was comparing the provisions of this fund with those of a bank, and he said that there was no comparison.
There is not.
Why? Do not the bank employees pay into a fund? Do not the banks also pay?
I do not know that they do.
Then do not contradict me.
I do not think the banks pay into the fund.
I think they do. I say I have known cases, and I know it is their policy whenever they dismiss a man to return his contributions.	.
Sortie banks do not contribute.
Some of them do, and the case is on all fours with this. I say there is no justice in this parliament passing a law to retain a man's money to which he is justly entitled.

speechtext:

act or not. We are extending it again now. My hon. friends opposite offer some objection. My hon. friend from Muskoka-Ontario brings up certain grievances, but he offers nothing constructive. Do they want the contributor's pension reduced? If they do, let them say so, and we will consider it.
I want the parties to pay who are going to benefit-. The government ought to pay it.
The government does not benefit. The government is a contributor.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I repeat, we have pointed out to the civil service representatives, who came to us no later than this week, that it was getting late in the session, and that we were not sure that we could . get this measure through. I told them frankly that I did not propose to stay here all summer to try to put this measure through, but I am ready to listen to anything constructive. If hon. gentlemen are simply going to find fault, and raise the case of one man here and another man there who wants his money back after voluntarily contributing to the fund, and they are not prepared to offer anything constructive, I shall have to tie the bill up so that we can consider during the year what would be the effect from an actuarial standpoint. We would have to consider how much more the government would have to contribute in that case, because either the government or the other civil servants would have to contribute more if the present scale of pensions is to be continued.

I understood the minister to say that the man went into the scheme voluntarily, and now he wants his money back. I think it all depends on circumstances. It is true he went into the scheme voluntarily and made his contributions, but it was on the expectation that he would remain in the service until such time as he would be eligible for superannuation. But he has be*n dismissed, and all he asks is that you pay him back, not wha-t you contributed, but what he contributed himself.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend is a good
business man, but he has missed the point. I have pointed out that in the experience of the Treasury Board we have discovered that some people were actually seeking dismissal so that they might get their money back.

Civil Service Superannuation Act

I am not dealing with such a man at all, but with the man who comes into the service and contributes voluntarily because he expects to stay in the service long enough to get the 'benefit of superannuation. You dismiss him and confiscate what he contributed. All he asks is that you return to him, not what you put in, but what he contributed himself. What is the answer to that?

When a man is
dismissed, does he not get back the money he contributed?

No, not under the new
scheme.
What is the answer?

The Minister of Trade and Commerce dismisses my plea in favour of this particular man by the assertion that the principle on which all superannuation acts are based is that some men in particular circumstances must lose and others gain, that those wTho leave the service within ten years must contribute five per cent of their salary to the pension fund for the benefit of those more fortunate who are permitted to remain in the service. That, in effect, is what he says. I want to point out where he is wrong. My complaint is not against the act. The act is all right. My complaint is against the ruling of the Treasury Board. The Minister of Finance implies that those of us who are criticizing have offered nothing constructive. I want nothing more constructive than the act itself; the act is quite satisfactory. Let me read subsection 3 of section 10 of the act:
Nothing herein contained. shall be understood as impairing or affecting the right of the governor in council to dismiss or remove any contributor from the civil service, and on such dismissal or removal the governor in council may, on the recommendation of the Treasury Board pay to the contributor the whole or any part of his contribution under this act as may be deemed expedient.
Can the Minister of Finance or the Minister of Trade and Commerce say that the act was based on the principle that a man in this position should not have his contributions to the fund returned? How can they make that assertion in view of that particular clause in the act? What I complain about is that after this act is passed and after all the arrangements are made the Treasury Board takes it on itself to make a ruling. This ruling is dated December 17, 1926, and it specifically deals with this case. It leaves this man outside the operations of the act. I am not complaining of the act itself. Some hon.
fMr Robb.]
member has asked that this document be read. It is rather a lengthy document, but I think I had better read it all. It reads:
The board had under consideration sundry submissions recommending, under the provisions of section 10 (3) of the Civil Service Superannuation Act, 1924, repayment of the contributions of employees dismissed or removed from the service. They also considered a memorandum prepared by the superintendent of insurance, at the request of the board, as to the advisability of authorizing such refunds.
The superintendent of insurance reported:
1.	That this provision was not intended to apply generally to all cases of dismissal.
I would ask my hon. friend to take particular note of that first clause.
That this provision was not intended to apply generally to all cases of dismissal.
Then section 2 reads:
2.	That employees with less than ten years' service cannot obtain refund of their contributions upon resignation; that consequently, it would be advantageous to such employees to be dismissed.
And section 3 reads:
3.	That the benefits under the act had been fixed on the understanding that there would be accruing to the fund, the contributions of employees retiring with less than ten years' service; and that if these contributions are not retained, the basis for maintenance of the fund would be destroyed. _
The board, concurring in the report and recommendation of the superintendent of insurance, are of opinion that:
1.	Refund of contributions should not be authorized to employees with less than ten years' service, who are dismissed or removed from the service.
That covers this particular case. I submit the act was not based on that principle, because the subsection I have read states clearly that the government shall have the right to refund the amount paid in by such employees. Certainly no one can claim the act was based on that. I can quite understand persons now in the service maintaining that that provision should be carried out. Why, an acceptance of the principle embodied in the ruling of the Treasury Board simply means confiscation of part of the salaries of the unfortunate employees, which was intended to be left for them in their old age, their widows and orphans. The argument that the civil service is behind it is no argument at all. Parliament is above the civil service. It is the duty of parliament to give justice not only to the civil servants who have been in the service sufficiently long to draw their pensions, but also to the less fortunate employees who are dismissed before they have been ten years in the service, and a part of whose salary is confiscated.

Civil Service Superannuation Act

My hon. friend referred to the privilege of appealing to the Treasury Board. There was the case submitted to the committee of the man who might be dismissed through the abolition of his office, although he had committed no offence against the department in which he worked. The man who retires voluntarily loses his contributions under the act; the man who commits some offence relating to his position oi against the department is not supposed to get his money back, 'but. the man whose position is abolished has the right of appeal and the Treasury Board may return to him his contributions.

That confirms what I
said; apparently the act intended to make a refund to employees who were dismissed.

No, except where a man was dismissed without cause, such as the abolition of the office, where there -was no offence on his part. I may point out to my hon. friend that immediately after the war representations were made that we had a very large civil service. Of course some departments would naturally become less heavily manned as years went by. Where a man had to be let out through the abolition of the office, having done nothing wrong himself, he should be allowed to get his money back.

The act does not say
that.
No.

In any case of dismissal the governor in council has the right to make a refund of the amount paid in. But the minister states there was an afterthought, that this is something that came up afterwards: that an employee who wanted to leave the office and avail himself of the opportunity could perhaps use his fists with his superiors and gets around the act. We have a ruling of the Treasury Board on that. What the minister says confirms my opinion that the act was not intended to apply as it was applied in the case to which I refer. If it was found out afterwards that is was simply tempting the employee who wanted1 to leave the service to be dismissed, then I maintain the government should have dealt with it in some other way to render justice to those who were dismissed.
What other way?
That he should ask the Treasury Board to carry out the original intention of the act. That is all I am arguing. I am complaining of the ruling of the Treasury Board; I am not complaining of the aot.

I am a member of the Treasury Board, and as such have had to consider, along with the other members of the board, cases of this kind. The abuse which the Treasury Board sought to correct under the section my hon. friend referred to arose from the fact that an employee who retires voluntarily with less than ten years' service should not have his contributions returned. My hon. friend will admit that proposition.
That is covered by the act.
Yes.
I am not complaining of that, but I am complaining of the interpretation given to the act by the Treasury Board in cases of dismissal.

We find this abuse existing: that men knowing that if they retire voluntarily, having served for a period under ten years, they could not receive their contribution, did something which compelled dismissal. So that there had to be consideration by the Treasury Board of the circumstances of dismissal in each case, as to whether or not the circumstances were such as to warrant the return of the contributions. There is hardly a meeting of the Treasury Board at which matters of dismissal and the relationship of the fund to these dismissals have not come before it for consideration, and there has to be a complete file of the circumstances in each case to enable the board to decide whether it is a proper case for the return of the contributions. There are other classes of cases. There are men who have been dismissed on account of defalcations, and when such a case arises it has to be shown to the board that that was the cause of dismissal. Does my hon. friend suggest that there should not be discretion somewhere in order to determine whether, even in cases of dismissal, contributions should or should not be returned? I submit that the discretion is absolutely necessaiy. So far as the general plan is concerned, it is in fact a pool. A man who puts his money into this scheme does not do so expecting to get more out of it than his contributions. The principle of pooling is the maximum good of all those participating in the pool. Some must bear a greater share of the burden in order that there may be equal benefits in case of disability or old age. There is no way of over-toming that inequality unless we adopt the annuity principle. Then unquestionably the payments either from the government or the contributors, or both, would have to be substantially larger than under this scheme.

Mr. Chairman, I submit that my contention is absolutely confirmed by the Minister of Railways. We have a frank admission from the treasury benches that as the act was framed the contributions of this class of employees were to be refunded. Therefore I submit that the contention of the Minister of Railways that the act was not framed with that in view is not correct. The present policy of not refunding in such cases is an afterthought.

Apparently the discretionary powers are entirely taken away. I claim that any employee is entitled to have the act carried out in the spirit in which it was framed.

If the hon. member will recall when this act was passed he would know that the committee to which it was referred was composed equally of members from each side of the House, because at the time the government had not a decided majority. The committee unanimously recommended the bill and it was enacted. When it came into the House the then Minister of . Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) offered no criticism. In fact the only criticism came from the then leader of the opposition, Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, who said that the measure was very generous, but he shuddered to think of the payments that the taxpayers would have to assume. If we had wanted to be more generous we would have to ask a large contribution either from the civil servants or the government.
May I again point out that I am not complaining of the act at all?
Carried.

It is not carried and
will not be for a while if that practice is indulged in. I protest against the Minister of Finance threatening to throw this bill over because we attempt to improve it. I am not particularly concerned about our civil servants. I think they are pretty well paid and protected in every shape and form, and I do not. think their work is very hard. Many a man in this country has got a day's work done before the civil servants commence their

duties. I am not complaining of that, for I know that the nature of the work is such that it must be transacted during certain hours. But the Minister of Railways has brought up a subject which to my mind is very important. I do not see what principle he could introduce into the Civil Service Act that would be more destructive of the morale of the service. He admits it himself and says that there is trouble every day. When people think that they are not getting what belongs to them they are going to fight for their rights, and I think he will continue to have trouble so long as this clause remains.

Mr. Chairman, I did not say that we have trouble, I said the Treasury Board has to deal with cases for the return of contributions to dismissed men. That is simply carrying out the intent of the act, it is not trouble. The only way to avoid it, as I pointed out, is to change the basis of the scheme, and provide that anyone, wdiether dismissed or retiring voluntarily, shall get his contributions refunded. In order to accomplish this the state would have to pay more and the contributors considerably more than they are now paying. We cannot carry on the scheme actuarily at the present rate of contribution if we admit that those who retire voluntarily or otherwise shall get their payments back.

Probably I am mistaken, but I thought I distinctly heard the minister say that at nearly every meeting of the Treasury Board they have to consider these cases. If that does not indicate trouble I do not know what does.

No, that is just the
ordinary business of the board.

To my mind the principle is wrong. If the government wants to do something for the civil service, let them do it, and let them call upon those civil servants who are going to participate in superannuation help to that end; but the principle of making them contribute a certain percentage of their salary and then retain those payments is wrong.

May I ask a question of the
Minister of Railways? He appears to be speaking for the Treasury Board.
No, I just butted in.

The House in committee on Bill No. 153, respecting the Baptist Convention of Ontario and Quebec-Mr. Edwards (Ottawa)-Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 1-Proviso.

maintopic: BAPTIST CONVENTION OF ONTARIO AND QUEBEC
speechtext:
I would like a
little explanation about this bill. I am rather surprised to see that there is no provision in it for protecting vested rights that have been acquired previous to this date. It seems to me that that is a very unusual omission from a bill of this kind.
Then I find that section 1 provides that the contention, on a three-fifths vote of the delegates present at any time, may pass a regulation that some of the delegates shall no longer be entitled to attend the convention, and that some of the churches may no longer select delegates for the convention.
I have received a communication from Laohute, which I did not get in time to present to the private bills committee yesterday, and as it expresses my views I shall take the liberty of reading it:
That the members of the Lachute Baptist Church hereby express their entire disapproval oi the amendment proposed to the act incorporating the Baptist Convention of Ontario and Quebec for the following among other reasons:
1.	That it is destructive of the independence of Baptist churches.
2.	That it would give to a three-fifths vote at any convention the power to declare by resolution what is or is not in harmony with the objects of the convention, while the resolution may be entirely out of harmony with, and destructive of, the principles and doctrines held by the denomination, and through this resolution absolutely to cut off any church from its vested rights as a free and independent Baptist church in the convention.
3.	That every Baptist church in the convention is possessed of vested rights in certain trust and endowment funds held for the work of the denomination, and the cutting off of any church from sending delegates to the convention would automatically nullify all their interest in the said endowment and trust funds.
4.	That it cloches the convention with such powers as would inevitably imperil the freedom of the ministry.

Baptist Convention
5.	That it would tend to bring the domestic affairs of the churches into discussion in the' convention, either to prove that a church is out of harmony with the convention, or to enable a disappointed minority in a church to appeal to the convention to justify themselves against the minister or pastor and the majority supporting him.
(Sgd) G. F. Calder. S. Goldsworthy,
Church Clerk.
I have no doubt, Mr. Chairman, that this bill has been carefully considered by the committee. I am not a member of the private bills committee myself, but it seems to me that these two objections to the bill are very serious ones. In the first place, there is no saving clause in regard to the vested rights of any community of the Baptist church, and further, it seems to me hardly in order that three-fifths of the members present at a convention should be able to pass a resolution excluding the delegates from some of the Baptist churches, or a resolution that certain Baptist churches should no longer have the right to send delegates to the convention.
I should like to have some explanation of these matters from some member of the committee here who is conversant with them.

maintopic: BAPTIST CONVENTION OF ONTARIO AND QUEBEC
speechtext:
I am perhaps not too conversant with the facts out of which this bill has arisen, but the sponsor for the bill is not here tonight, and he asked me if it did come up to say a word in explanation to the committee.
I am sorry that my hon. friend from Argenteuil was not at the committee, because I can assure him that if he had been there he would have listened for at least three hours to a complete discussion of all the points to which he has referred by gentlemen who were thoroughly in touch with them and would have been able to give him very much more close range information than I can.
In a word, the purpose of the bill, as I understand it, is to bring the organization known as the Baptist Convention of Ontario and Quebec into line with the organizations of that body existing in other parts of Canada. I understand that the Baptist convention is incorporated in British Columbia and the western provinces, and there they have the usual powers of any domestic corporation as to discipline, as to the conduct of their affairs, and who shall send delegates. Down in the maritimes, particularly in New Brunswick, there is a similar act of incorporation, but the Maritime Baptist Convention is not, I understand, incorporated as a convention.
I would draw the attention of the committee to this, that a convention which is not incorporated has, I think, in law the power
to do exactly what is suggested in the section to which my hon. friend has referred, so that all that is sought here is to supply an omission in the old act of 1889, in which it is provided that each regular church is entitled to send delegates, and nothing is said whatever as to the disciplinary powers which may be possessed by the convention, in case it becomes necessary or is thought advisable to use those powers. In the case of any club or domestic organization, its domestic affairs are under its control, but I understand that this body is advised that because of this omission there is doubt whether they have power to control who shall and who shall not send delegates to the convention. The purpose of this section is to supply that omission.
With regard to property rights, may I just say a word? The Baptist churches throughout the world are autonomous bodies. Each church owns its own property. The convention or the cooperative assembly through which they work has no property whatever, and has no interest in the property of the churches, so the body which is incorporated here holds no property, and has no interest in the property of the individual churches, and all that the churches may do, and the only interest they may have in the cooperative work, is to send delegates who can vote on various matters that come before the convention, with regard to the good of the denomination and relating to the objects for which the convention is brought together. In that connection 1 want the committee to have the fullest information, because there are two or three boards which are appointed by the convention, namely, a board to hold funds for the home missions, a board to hold and administer funds for foreign missions, and a board to administer superannuation funds for aged and infirm ministers. The convention as such has no property in the fund whatever. The funds are contributed by the individual churches and all the convention does is to nominate the members of the board. My hon. friend from Argenteuil probably does not know also that under the act which incorporated McMaster university this convention is authorized to appoint a board to deal with matters pertaining to that educational institution. That is not under this act, but under the act incorporating McMaster university, and so, as was pointed out before the committee, in connection with the question of property rights it would seem as though those who go to vote at the convention have no more interest in the property which is being administered by those boards whom they elect than the persons comprising the governor in
Baptist Convention

council which elects the board of the Canadian National Railways would have in the property of the Canadian National Railways. I therefore think that the suggestion which was made to the committee is sound, that if you insert what is called a saving clause with respect to property you give some astute lawyer an opportunity of saying " Well, parliament must have thought, notwithstanding the apparent plain provisions of the act, that there was some property interest somewhere ", and probably an argument would be founded on that basis. I submit that it would be unwise and unnecessary to insert such a provision, because if you look at the proviso proposed it is purely a section for the purpose of excluding the church from sending delegates to the convention and does not purport to affect property. I submit there is no such thing as property in this concern, and the operation of this association is such that it does not normally acquire property.
The other proposition was as to the three-fifths vote. My suggestion to the committee is that the usual procedure for action by such a corporation is to proceed by a majority vote-majority in matters of discipline as well as matters in connection with property and the general affairs of the corporation. In this case I understand that it was the idea of the promoters of the bill that whoever it dealt with might be assured that there was no desire captiously to interfere with the attendance of anybody at the association, and so the three-fifths majority was suggested. In the ordinary case I think it would be fifty per cent.
I desire to refer to another matter. Under the provisions of this act it does not come into force until it is ratified by the convention itself, which gives full notice to all interested of the possibility of action under this legislation. Although I am a member of the denomination, I do not happen to be a member of this convention. I understand there are some 508 churches in the convention and that a protest, was received-any hon. member can correct mei if I am wrong-or sent in by thirty-five churches to the people who are opposing this bill. The further statement was made that a protest has been received from individual members of 120 churches in all but when it was analyzed it was found that that rtieant that one individual member of a church might count as one of the 120. So that I think as the matter stands the bill represents _ the desire of 508 churches, with the exception of 35, and with the exception of some individual members from some 85 other churches.

speechtext:
My hon. friend
says there are no property rights involved, and I am quite sure he is stating it as he understands it. Sometimes errors are made in a matter of this kind. I do suggest, therefore, being a member of the bar myself, that it would be unwise and would be unduly casting a cloud on this association if we insisted that, as a condition to this corporation getting the power that other corporations have, they should have. something added that would in a lefthanded way suggest that somebody had ' property rights when apparently none exist.

speechtext:
