I want to direct to the attention of the minister now in charge of the bill a concrete case which has been submitted to me. Suppose a civil servant should die, say, six days before the expiry of the ten year period which is necessary to entitle his dependents to superannuation. I understand that it is the practice at present to pay to the dependents of civil servants who die during the month the full amount of salary for that month. If that were done in the case I am supposing-and this is not a hypothetical case, for it has been brought to my notice only to-day-would not the fact that the salary would be paid for the full month extend the time of service of the deceased so as to complete the ten year period? What is the minister's interpretation of the statute in regard to this point? Would the dependents, under such circumstances as these, be entitled to the allowance?

By the way, who is in
charge of the bill?

The bill stands in the
name of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), but I understand that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) is familiar with the subject. There was a good deal of discussion this afternoon which I think might be continued in the absence of the Minister of Finance.
Will the minister give an estimate of what the bill will eventually cost the country?

First of all I should like to have an answer to the point I have brought forward. As I say, this is not a hypothetical case; it has actually come to my notice. A civil servant dies six days before the end of his ten year period, and the present practice is to pay his salary up to the end of the month in' which he dies. Does the minister think that this practice would apply to the payment of the superannuation allowance so as to complete the ten year period? I should like to know whether the minister thinks that in that case the dependents would be eligible to receive the allowance.
1794	COMMONS
Civil Service Superannuation Act

I do not see that it would make much difference whether death occurred one month or one year before the end of the period. I agree with imy hon. friend that it does seem an injustice to deprive the dependents of the allowance which they would otherwise receive, merely because the man died just a few days before the necessary time had elapsed. However, the ten year period is arbitrary, and the same problem would arise no matter what length of time we might fix.

But I am pointing out that the present practice in the payment of salaries is to grant the salary to the end of the month in which the civil servant dies. If that same practice were observed in the case I have cited the result 'would be to extend the time of service so as to complete the requisite period.
The date of death determines the status of the beneficiary.

As I understand the act, the civil servant is not entitled to repayment of moneys paid in unless he has been, in the service the full ten years. It seems to me that anyone who becomes incapacitated or who is removed by the department from any cause other than misconduct as set out in subsection 1 should be entitled to receive what he has contributed.

I do not believe my hon. friend was in the House this afternoon when the mattf^- was discussed. Certain objections were raised which appeared to be well taken. However, the purpose of the bill is to provide certain benefits for civil servants. When the bill was first introduced that question was very carefully considered. It has to be admitted that the benefits of the money paid in do not accrue to those retiring after a service of less than ten years. In case of dismissal, as has been pointed out this afternoon, the Treasury Board has discretionary power to review the case. As the Minister of Finance pointed out, to add provisions to the bill conferring any further benefits would really entail a complete revision of the assessment necessary to provide the payments. Therefore I do not think the committee would be well advised to disturb the principle of the bill at this stage.
The minister spoke of those dismissed for misconduct, but what about those who have become incapacitated? Should not provision be made for them?

The bill provides for
those who become disabled within the ten year period.
fMr. MarLaren.]

Will those employees who

On section 2-Application of part I.

I think this is the appropriate place to bring before the government and the House the claim of two small bodies, in the one case of civil servants and in the other of persons who ought to be classed as civil servants, to come under this act. This is not a revolutionary matter or a suggestion to change the basis of the act. It involves no greater contribution or no less superannuation allowance. Possibly it involves a little extra

Civil Service Superannuation Act
expense on the part of the government, but only in the regular proportion which the government contributes under the act. The amount is small because they are two small bodies. If they had not been small bodies numerically and serving the country in remote-places, perhaps their claim would have been considered before now. If they had numbered two or three thousand and lived in Ottawa, the justice of their case would have ensured that it receive consideration before- now. The one case is a matter of including civil servants who are now really civil servants but who are not allowed superannuation. The other is a matter of including as civil servants people who should be classed as civil servants, and I cannot for the life of me understand why they are not so classed. I have in my hand a very modestly drawn up petition from the officers of the ships of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, -a petition which in polite and respectful language sets forth their case. The trouble with these men is that they are prohibited from being members of the civil service because the Civil Service Act contains a section which reads:
This act shall not apply to any position on any ship of His Majesty until parliament otherwise enacts.
Of course, not being civil servants, they do not come under the Superannuation Act. It is unnecessary for me to argue or stress the advisability of giving superannuation to civil servants, because that has been conceded all along the line and that is what this act is about. We will therefore commence with the premises that it is just and proper that men in the service of the country should be encouraged, .by looking forward to superannuation, to stay with their department and give it the value of their experience. These men are prevented from doing that. They have to do a great deal of rather strenuous work. They serve the fisheries protection service and also the lighthouse service. They are out in all sorts of weather and under very strenuous conditions. They are expected at times to risk their lives in the performance of their duties. This is not a particularly nice service, and it is the very type of service that makes it highly desirable for the government to encourage them to stay with it because their experience is worth a great deal more than that of a man in a merely clerical position.
I am more familiar with the Pacific coast, and I know that the knowledge which these men must acquire in performing their duties makes it eminently desirable that the government should encourage them to remain in the service

instead of having the best men picked up by the commercial companies because of their usefulness. I do not suppose more then sixty or seventy men would be involved so that the expense would be small. If they were made civil servants, they would be eligible for superannuation. That covers that phase of the question.
The other class to which I wish to refer is that of telegraphists, agent operators, agent linesmen and linesmen in the government telegraph service. They may be a little more numerous. They are prohibited, for a totally different reason, from enjoying the benefits of superannuation. Those who are telegraphists, agent operators or agent linesmen are all civil servants, appointed by the Civil Service Commission, so that with the exception of linesmen they are all civil servants, and they are certainly permanent because they continue in the service for twenty or thirty years. Why are they not allowed to enjoy the benefits of superannuation?
In the case of the employees of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment the argument used for prohibiting them was that the department was only a temporary establishment which would in time pass away, and the government did not want to have the heavy responsibility of pensioning these people after only a few years' service. But people of the class to which I am now referring continue in the service practically all their lives. I know of oases of both men and women telegraphists who have been twenty-five years in the service, and who, if they are laid off to-morrow, will not get a cent of pension. Many of these people do not appreciate the position they are -in because they have been drifting along under the benefits of the Calder Act under which a number were superannuated and received a reasonable superannuation. Many of them hardly grasp the fact that when the Calder Act under which they were eligible for superannuation was done away with, they were no longer eligible under this superannuation act. The quibble, for I can hardly call it anything -else, which was employed to deny them the right to come in under the superannuation act like other civil servants was this. Some brilliant genius invented the theory that they were not paid a stated annual salary and the act states that only those are eligible who are in receipt of a stated annual salary. The fact that these salaries are paid monthly does not seem to make any difference. Some of them have been paid for twenty-five years. For instance, a woman has drawn her stated annual salary, receiving it month by month, received her annual holiday and every-

Civil Service Superannuation Act
thing else; she is a permanent civil servant; but because of this beautiful theory that she was drawing what was called current wages and not a stated annual salary, she was declared ineligible. That is a mere quibble that should be set right. These people are not drawing current wages because that would suggest that the amount was fluctuating from month to month; that if the market was a little brisk, we would expect to see their wages increase. These people like all other civil servants receive an annual salary paid monthly and the amount of their salary will be found year out and year in, in the Auditor General's report. Now because of that theory, that obsession I might almost call it, that they are not being paid a stated annual salary, they are not allowed to come in. I think that is practically the whole case, and it needs only to be stated, I think, to show the injustice they are suffering. I hope that if the minister in charge of this bill cannot see his way to insert this amendment, which would not involve much trouble or expense, he will at least give us the assurance that he will consider the matter during the recess with the prospect or the intention of bringing these people in next year. But I would like to hear the minister's view as to why these two classes of men are not eligible to come under this act.

The hon. gentleman has both asked and answered the question. The answer he gave was the very answer which I would have given. They were not included because none of the prevailing-rates men were included, and they were treated at the time the bill was introduced as being prevailing-rates men. To give my hon. friend the assurance that their case would be reconsidered would not be very difficult for me, because I recall distinctly that some of us on the committee at the time were of the opinion that some further consideration should be given to the prevailing-rates men who were kept on permanently year after year, and were in receipt of what was practically an annual salary, although it was not regarded as such. This bill provides for the payment of annuities to widows of contributors to superannuation funds Nos. 1 and 2 who died in service or after superannuation.

Will the minister give us some information about section 21?

That was passed the last
time the bill was before the House.
On section 25-Being on board of smuggling vessel.
I move that section 25 be struck out. There is no necessity for it.
Is this part of the retreat?

No. We had thought of
making every person found on board a boat carrying smuggled goods prove he was innocent of smuggling. Perhaps it is going a little too far, and I am willing to have the section struck out.

We have learned that
people on boats are not always guilty.

Motion agreed to.
On section 37-Counsel fees.
I move to strike out this section. It merely has reference to fixing counsel fees in the discretion of the court, and has nothing whatever to do with smuggling.
Have you any more lawyers you wish to appoint as counsel?

Motion agreed to.
On section 38-Maximum penalty.

I move that we strike out subsection 2 of 285A section 38. That deals
1S06
Canada Grain Act

with the powers of magistrates to suspend sentence. We thought it was a little severe. AVe are quite willing to leave it to the judges whether a sentence be suspended or not.
It has been suggested that instead of imposing a penalty for the offence we should give a medal to those who get through with it.
Will my hon. friend donate one?

Motion agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 39-Distribution of proceeds.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
An amendment was moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre-
That all the words after the word "repealed" ill the nineteenth line to the word "forfeiture" in the twenty-sixth line be struck out.

I ask the committee not to insist on this amendment. It deals with the matter of informers and the paying of informers. There is great difficulty in getting these informers to work if they do not receive their pay quickly after giving the information. It is most unfortunate that we have to use these men, but it is necessary. This has particular reference to the matter of informing in regard to the smuggling of liquor, and it usually becomes advisable for the informer not to remain in the neighbourhood long after he gives the information, yet he ought to be paid.
Were we not informed that the person who lays the information respecting the smuggling of liquor receives no money at all?
If the liquor is sold he certainly gets his share of the proceeds.

The liquor or the cash?
Amendment (Mr. Woodsworth) negatived.

Section agreed to.
Section 40 agreed to.
Preamble and title agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture, for the Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved the second reading of Bill No. 235, to amend the Canada Grain Act.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
Sections 1 and 2 agreed to.
Does this bill cover all the amendments that it is intended to make to the Canada Grain Act?

Yes. '
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

Hon. P. J. A. CARDIN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) moved the second reading of Bill No. 226 relating to the harbour of St. John in the province of New Brunswick.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 1.

Mr. Chairman, after some conversation with the Minister of Railways I understood that his was the first bill to come up to-night and that none of these harbour bills would be dealt with. The members interested have, I think, left the chamber on that understanding.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: If my hon. friend does not wish to proceed with this bill we can take up another, but I may say to him that the bill dealing with the Halifax harbour is almost verbatim et literatim with this, and we thought that if we could get through one of them to-night we might save that much time.

If the member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) has no objection, and the Prime Minister is agreeable, we might dispose of this bill with the exception of one clause, for I think the member for St. John-1 Albert (Mr. MacLaren) would like to be present before the measure is finally disposed of. Maybe the minister in charge of the bill can give us an explanation of its purpose.

Mr. Chairman, this bill is simply to incorporate the harbour commission of St. John along the same lines as the harbour commissions of Montreal and Vancouver, and it contains practically the same clauses as are in the acts relating to those two harbours. We might proceed with the bill, and if it contains anything which is not satisfactory to my hon. friend we can reserve it to be dealt with when we reach the third reading. I may say that the bill has been submitted to the city council of St. John and they have accepted it.

St. John Harbour Commission
I do not doubt at all what the minister says, but I should like the member for St. John to state his views. I observe that he is here now.
I understand, Mr. Chairman, that the mayor and city council of St. John are willing to accept the bill as drawn.

I might add that recently I had an interview here with representatives of the city council of St. John and they are favourable to the bill. Besides that, the mayor has wired me that he is perfectly satisfied with its terms. There is necessity for immediate action on the adoption of this bill because the legislature of the province is sitting, and should this bill pass they will have to enact legislation empowering the city of St. John to conduct a plebiscite under its act of incorporation. If there is no serious objection to any of the clauses, it would be well to put the bill through to-night so that the legislature could be advised on Monday and proceed with their legislation.

I trust that we will
proceed with the bill now. There are many urgent reasons for putting the bill through at the earliest opportunity.

I am quite agreeable to the passage of the bill. I was simply waiting until the members directly interested were in their seats. The city of St. John owns a very substantial amount of harbour property. Is there any provision in the bill for taking it over? If so, at what price?
Yes, at an agreed price of $2,135,000.
I have not had an opportunity to look over the bill. Will the control of grain operations fall under the jurisdiction of the Board of Grain Commissioners?
That is my information.

Under the regulations they
have power to make any rules for handling the traffic of the port.

I am anxious to see this bill pass, but the success or failure of the harbour under a commission will depend very largely on the cost to be borne by the traffic going through the port. Does this bill provide that the tolls or rates to be charged by the harbour commission shall be subject, to the approval of the governor in council?
Yes.
I should like an answer to my inquiry, Mr. Chairman.
My understanding is that the grain traffic in the local elevators will be under the control of the grain board.
Are the tolls charged by the harbour commission subject' to approval by the governor in council?

Yes, the tolls have to be
approved.
Is that the case with regard to the Vancouver harbour board?
That is the case with all harbours. [DOT]

I do not think the Vancouver harbour commission is under the jurisdiction of the department so far as the operation of elevators is concerned. The tariffs charged by the elevators are not subject to the approval of the governor in council and when any change is required it is simply referred to the Board of Grain Commissioners.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
My hon.
friend is speaking of the grain elevators?
Yes.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: That is different from the harbour commission. In that particular case the elevators are operated by the harbour board. Of course, tolls charged by the elevators are subject to the Board of Grain Commissioners.

Is it the general policy to confer powers of expropriation upon harbour commissions? Powers of expropriation are extreme, and I see by section 13 that this power is conferred on the corporation. I appreciate the fact that it mav be necessary, but in such legislation passed in the province of New Brunswick it is customary where this power is granted to make it subject to the approval of tlhe lieutenant governor in council. Of course, if that is not the practice in Dominion legislation I have no objection, but if this is a departure I think the approval of the governor in council should be required.
This provision appears in the other acts. It involves capital expenditure which of course must be passed on by the governor in council.
I appreciate that, but it is hardly the point I make.

An understanding
has been arrived at, I believe, between the city of St. John and the minister, and the terms of the bill as presented are quite satisfactory. I should however like to make a suggestion here with regard to tolls. I have

St. John Harbour Commission

been asked by the city council to find out whether it would be possible for the government to consider including in the bill the following provision:
Rates, tolls and charges for the conduct of business shall not at present be imposed in excess of those now in force and such rates, tolls and charges shall be fixed from time to time so as to enable the port of Saint John to compete successfully with other ports and places on the Atlantic seaboard in the United States of America or elsewhere.

It would not be practical to fix the rates, which must depend upon the circumstances of the port. If we' fixed the rates 'by statute we should be obliged to come back to parliament to make suich changes as might be found necessary. The rates are determined by the commission and submitted to the governor in council for approval, and that I think is the proper way to deal with the matter.
Mr. MaoLAREN: I understand that the provisions of this bill are similar to those in other acts relating to harbour commissions.
Absolutely.
The rates will be fixed by the port of St. John, in whom the city council will have faith.

I do not think there is any desire on the part of the city to introduce any contentious question. In the past there has been some trouble in the matter of rates and the city council would like to have something definite enacted in (his regard. However, if that is not possible the bill as drawn will be satisfactory. I do not bring the question up for the purpose of criticizing the bill.

This bill is framed to meet the recommendations of the Duncan commission, before whom representatives of St. John appeared and gave evidence. As regards the rates to be charged, I think we may safely leave this matter to the harbour commission; they will undoubtedly look after the interests of the port of S't. John. The commission will comprise men residing in the locality and taking a special interest in the development of the port, and it is only natural to assume (hat they will frame their schedule in such a way as to attract trade to the port. It is much better, I think, to leave the matter to a commission of local men rather than to officers residing in Ottawa. We should have some confidence in the men who are to be appointed as commissioners and we can safely rely on them.

That explanation
is satisfactory.

The minister will agree
that the success or failure of the traffic through the port will depend on whether the tolls are reasonable or excessive.
Certainly.

And naturally (he rates
will be made as attractive as possible. I have no further objection to offer.

With reference to the
question raised by the hon. member for Lethbridge, as to whether any elevators that may be established will come under the grain commissioners, I would remind the minister that in 1925 when the new grain act went through -I am speaking from memory of course- provision was made for putting all harbour commission elevators under the control of that board. It may be necessary to include in this bill a section putting in the same category the elevators in this case. I will look up the act of 1925 and in the meantime perhaps the minister will let this section stand.

On the third reading of
the bill we can deal with my hon. friend's suggestion.
That will be satisfactory.

Section agreed to.
Sections 2 to 5 inclusive agreed to.
On section 6-Harbour limits defined.
Are there any parts of the harbour that are exempted?

None excepting the ferry
landing and certain lots for fishing purposes.

Section agreed to.
On section 13-Expropriation of land.

Is not the expropriation
power given to the corporation in this section too wide? If the power to expropriate is made subject to the approval of the governor in council I shall 'be perfectly satisfied. In New Brunswick it has not been customary to grant such power to private corporations or public corporations without the consent of the governor in council. That is the only suggestion I have to make with regard to this clause.

The clause as framed is
practically a reproduction of the clause which appears in the statutes relating to other har-

1S09
St. John Harbour Commission
hour commissions. We thought it would not be fair to place the harbour commission of St. John in a different position from that of other harbour commissions.

Well, I have thrown out
the suggestion.

Section agreed to.
Sections 14 to 32 inclusive agreed to.
On the preamble.

Before the preamble is
carried I would ask if there should not be a provision in the bill for an annual audit of accounts of the harbour board?

There is already provision
for an audit in the Revenue and Audit Act. My hon. friend will also find that there is provision in one of the clauses for an officer of the Marine and Fisheries department making an investigation and audit of the books and affairs of the harbour commission. I think therefore, that the question of an audit is already adequately provided for. However, the matter can be raised again on the third reading of the bill if my hon. friend deems it necessary to take that course.

It is quite proper that
an officer of the department should make an independent audit, but what I had reference to more particularly was the desirability of an annual audit. If the minister will find out whether these harbour commissions come under the Audit Act and will let us know when the bill comes up for third reading, I think that will be satisfactory.

I can state to my hon.
friend now that they do come under the Audit Act.

There is another point
I may as well bring forward at this particular time, and that is that members of the House should have a little more information with regard to the financial standing of these harbour commissions, which are very important bodies having the control of public property. But we do not get any reports from them as to their financial condition and how they carry on their business. I would suggest to the minister that it might be advisable to supply hon. members with a copy of the annual statement of the different harbour commissions so that we can get in better touch with the business they are doing. I am satisfied that would save a good deal of trouble both to the minister and to the commisioners
themselves. If we are in possesion of full information on these matters we would prdb-ably not be so suspicious as we are sometimes inclined to be.

I think it is already
provided that information of the character asked for shall be supplied to members of the House.

In that case I shall
only ask that the minister ascertain whether an audit is provided for under the Audit Act and give us that information when the motion for third reading is made.

I feel sure that provision
for an audit of the accounts of harbour commissions is made in the Audit Act, but I will ascertain beyond doubt and inform my hon. friend.
Is it an independent audit or a departmental audit?
It is made by the Board of Audit which has been created to carry out work of that character.

If that is so it should be
satisfactory.

I think there is an error
in section 25 which I have just noticed. It is provided that the corporation may "in the following cases seize and detain any vessel within the limits of the province of Nova Scotia''. That is manifestly an error.

In my copy of the bill it
is "New Brunswick''.
My copy is wrong then.

In my copy it reads
"within the limits of the province of New Brunswick".
Mr, CARDIN:	Then the error has been
corrected in other copies of the bill.

May I draw the minister's attention to the fact that the bay of Fundy is partly within the province of New Brunswick and partly within the province of Nova Scotia and that it has been looked upon as a mare clausum. Has the minister given any consideration to that matter? I am just suggesting it for his consideration.

I will give consideration to that point.
Preamble agreed -to.
Bill reported.

Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 230, to amend the Special AArar Revenue Act, 1915.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
Section 1 agreed to.
On section 2-Power to determine fair price.

Will the minister explain the last paragraph in section 2?
fMr. Cardin.]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In some cases companies have set up subsidiary organizations to whom they sell their products, and taxes are paid on values lower than the fair market price. The present section is designed to protect our revenues against this.

Section agreed to.
On section 3-Regulations.

Before we go on with this bill, might I suggest to the minister that the ex-Minister of Finance, the hon. member for AArest Calgary (Mr. Bennett) is not present. I have no particular objection to this bill going on provided that -we report progress on the last clause and, if necessary, allow any discussion on the last clause when the bill comes before the committee again. AA ill that be satisfactory?

speechtext: That will be all right.

Section agreed to.
Sections 4 to 7 inclusive agreed to.
' On section 8-Trustees, assignees, executors, et ceteTa, to obtain certificate that all charges are paid before distribution.

Hon. P. J. A. CARDIN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) moved the second reading of Bill No. 22.5, respecting the Halifax Harbour Commissioners.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 1.
These two bills respecting the harbour commissions at Halifax and St. John are not exactly the same. Will the minister explain the difference?

They are exactly the same except that in the case of St. John, the harbour was under the control of the city, was city property, and we had to assume certain obligations of the city of St. John. That was not the case in Halifax. That is the only difference.

Section agreed to.
Sections 2 to 17 inclusive agreed to.

Halifax Harbour Commission
On section 18-Borrowing powers.

I notice that in this
bill, as in the other one, we are granting certain borrowing powers. Does that mean that the commission will have power to float bonds and debentures, or will they have to come to this House just like the other commissions when they want to borrow money?

Everything they borrow
has to be approved by the governor in council. They can borrow money and give as a guarantee the revenue of the port, but all subject to the approval of the governor in council.
Is this a similar section to that contained in the other acts?
Yes.

It is to give the governor in council an opportunity of looking over the proposed borrowings, and probably to keep the commissioners from landing into the mess the Vancouver harbour commissioners got into?
We have the power to stop any borrowing.

Section agreed to.
Sections 19 to 27 inclusive agreed to.
On section 28-Powers of corporation not to be restricted by provincial statutes.

This section says:
Notwithstanding anything contained in any act of the late province of Nova Scotia or of the new province of Nova Scotia-
Might I ask what is meant by the late province of Nova Scotia and the new province?

That relates to certain
by-laws which have been passed by the city of Halifax with the authorization of the provincial government.

Section agreed to.
Section 29 agreed to.
On the preamble.
I presume the minister will give the same understanding here with regard to the elevators being brought under the grain commission?
Yes.

Preamble agreed to.
Bill reported.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There is one order here for the consideration of amendments made by the Senate to Bill No. 61, to amend the Soldier Settlement Act. The government is prepared to accept those amendments. and if hon. gentlemen opposite have no objections we might take that up now.

I do not think it will take any time at the next sitting of the House. I myself would not object but there are some members who are not present now who might wish to discuss them.
